summary.text:
Southwark's 2026-27 Investment Strategy went through Council Assembly on 25 February 2026 as a short and tightly-numbered pair of appendices — Appendix C is the prudential indicators, Appendix D is the investment framework. There is no rate view, no adviser commentary, no MRP policy statement, no narrative on the borrowing plan. Everything a lender would notice sits in Appendix C's Table 6 (the liability benchmark) and Table 3 (the balance sheet forecast).

The scale of the internal position is the standout. At forecast 31 December 2025, CFR of £2,025m against £1,205m of borrowing and £23m of other long-term liabilities leaves roughly £797m funded internally — 39% of the CFR. Under the plan in Table 3, that only reduces to about £644m by 2028/29, as external borrowing grows £416m against £266m of CFR growth. The plan draws £337m of new borrowing across three years but closes only about £416m of the £532m liability-benchmark gap Table 6 shows would open with no new borrowing at all. Table 6 arithmetic ties to the pound at every row.

Two other things are worth noticing. The HRA financing-cost ratio (Table 7) sits at 31% at 31/12/25 and drifts to 33% by 2028/29 — roughly a third of HRA net revenue absorbed by debt service, against 13-14% for the General Fund. And the maturity structure (Table 8) is long-dated legacy: only 9% under 24 months, but 60% beyond ten years and 37% in the 30-50 year buckets, almost certainly HRA-vintage PWLB drawn at pre-2010 rates. On the investment side (Appendix D), the single substantive change is doubling the UK Local Authorities sector limit from £50m to £100m — a signal that inter-authority lending is becoming a material line for Southwark on the placement side.

We do not have a clean loan-book reconciliation. Our PWLB file at 31/12/25 shows £568m across 54 loans against Table 3's single 'Borrowing' line of £1,205m — the gap is LOBOs, market debt and any other borrowing the paper carries under one heading. The paper does not disaggregate. That gap goes in the note, not the email.

officer.subject: £797m of your CFR is funded internally — and £644m of it stays there through 2028/29
officer.body:
Hi [name],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the 2026-27 pair — Appendix C on prudential indicators, Appendix D on investments — that went through Assembly on 25 February. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Appendix C is unusually tightly numbered; Table 6 does more work than most liability benchmark tables we see, which is where most of what follows starts.

The scale of the internal position is the first thing. At forecast 31 December 2025, CFR of £2,025m against £1,205m of borrowing and £23m of other long-term liabilities leaves roughly £797m funded from your own reserves and working capital — 39% of the CFR. Under the plan in Table 3 that falls to about £644m by 2028/29 as external borrowing grows £416m against £266m of CFR growth. Table 6 says the same thing differently — the £532m under-benchmark by 2028/29 is what you'd have with no new borrowing at all, and the plan closes about £416m of it. The liability benchmark is the one indicator that tells you when the internal position stops being the cheaper option, which is why we keep coming back to it in these notes.

The HRA financing-cost ratio is the second. Table 7 has it at 31% at 31 December 2025 drifting to 33% by 2028/29 — roughly a third of HRA net revenue on debt service, against 13-14% for the General Fund. It's on the higher end of what we've read this year, though we've read more General Fund reports than HRA ones so we'd want to be careful with that comparison.

The maturity shape is the third. Table 8 has 5% under 12 months and 4% in the 12-24 month bucket — call it £108m against a £1,205m book — with 37% in the 30-50 year buckets. Near-term refinancing pressure is genuinely low; the arithmetic that matters sits decades out, on loans mostly drawn at HRA-settlement-era coupons. Long-dated PWLB certainty rates today are a long way above those coupons, so most of that older book will be trading well below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve. We price every loan daily and the borrower view is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

One smaller thing from Appendix D. Doubling the UK Local Authorities sector limit from £50m to £100m (para 4) is the only substantive change from November, and inter-authority lending has been a growing line for treasurers on both sides — July 2026 was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. The monthly breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, the two most relevant to where Southwark sits are cost-of-carry and our liability benchmark pathway — the latter is interactive and built on live data, which matters given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members there's Audit Committee Chair (Treasury), written for exactly the committee your treasury reports go through. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
